# Ex vivo organotypic culture of liposarcoma effectively models in vivo supratherapeutic paclitaxel localized drug delivery

**Authors:** Ilaria Caturegli; Rong Liu; Victoria Rivera; Olivia Taub; Mark W Grinstaff; Yolonda L Colson; Chandrajit P Raut

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Surgery, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, 75 Francis St., Boston, MA, 02115, USA | bDivision of Thoracic Surgery, Department of Surgery, Mass General Brigham, 55 Fruit St., Boston, MA, 02114, USA | cDepartment of Engineering, Boston University, 44 Cummington Mall, Boston, MA, 02215, USA | dDivision of Surgical Oncology, Department of Surgery, Mass General Brigham, 75 Francis St., Boston, MA, 02115, USA

## Abstract

•Paclitaxel chemosensitivity in monolayer cell culture is unrelated to in vivo chemo-resistance.•Organotypic culture demonstrated chemo-resistance in vivo equivalent condition.•Paclitaxel cytotoxicity at high concentrations in organotypic culture may be caspase-sensitive.

Paclitaxel chemosensitivity in monolayer cell culture is unrelated to in vivo chemo-resistance.

Organotypic culture demonstrated chemo-resistance in vivo equivalent condition.

Paclitaxel cytotoxicity at high concentrations in organotypic culture may be caspase-sensitive.

## Abstract

Retroperitoneal sarcomas (RPS) exhibit a high locoregional recurrence rate after macroscopically complete surgical resection. Systemic therapies have limited efficacy and significant adverse effects. Sarcoma cell lines are susceptible to paclitaxel (PTX), a microtubule stabilizer, in 2-dimensional (2-D) monolayer cell culture, but resistant in animal models. When locally delivered via drug-eluting buttresses supratherapeutic concentrations are achieved and PTX becomes efficacious. Due to the limitations of 2-D culture, we establish an organotypic culture system to model the mechanisms by which supratherapeutic and prolonged exposure of PTX is effective.

Liposarcoma tumors (LP6) were established subcutaneously in NU/J mice. Tumors were harvested, sliced with a vibratome (250 µm thick), and cultured on permeable trans wells.

Organotypic culture viability was maintained up to 7 days with greater than 50 % viability. Tumor slices were composed of 82 % ± 7 % human liposarcoma cells with the remainder being mouse stroma as determined by CD44 staining. Under 4-day exposure, IC50 of PTX with organotypic culture shifted 7000 rightward as compared to 2-D culture. A subset of 17 genes was significantly differentially expressed as compared to untreated controls, while no genes were differentially expressed after 1 day of treatment. Gene set enrichment analysis demonstrated enrichment in apoptotic, extracellular matrix, cell motility, and cell cycle pathways. Caspase-8 activation occurred only at 10,000 ng/mL and 4-days of PTX or greater.

This study reports a reproducible, clinically relevant organotypic culture liposarcoma model, which can serve as an intermediary between in vitro and in vivo studies.

## Introduction

Traditional cancer in vitro models often fall short of the clinical parameters one needs to reproduce to probe the complexities of the biology and therapeutic susceptibilities of tumors. Organotypic culture allows for representative, yet modular study of the tumor microenvironment and its perturbations. Advantages of this model system, as compared to in vitro monolayer or in vivo animal models, include accurate representation of a complex tumor microenvironment, three-dimensional cell architecture and scaffold, cell division dynamics, and genetic mutational burden rate [1,2]. Most importantly, this culture methodology allows for the translation of patient-derived tumor biology to study a given tumor’s response to chosen therapies, thus allowing for selection and utilization of effective therapies in precision treatment for the patient.

Retroperitoneal sarcomas (RPS) are a family of locally aggressive soft-tissue malignancies with surgery as the only potentially curative treatment option. Curative resection is often difficult to achieve given inherent tumor biology and involvement of critical structures. (Neo)adjuvant systemic therapy, such as chemotherapy and radiotherapy, is relatively ineffective in most histologic types with response rates of only 10 % to 20 %, even with first-line systemic therapy [3]. Locoregional recurrence accounts for much of the morbidity and mortality, depending on histologic types, and represents an unmet therapeutic challenge.

While systemic administration of the chemotherapeutic agent paclitaxel (PTX), a microtubule stabilizer, has proven ineffective in most soft tissue sarcoma histologic types, implantable PTX-loaded polymer buttresses proved safe and effective in decreasing local sarcoma recurrence in a human sarcoma xenograft model in mice [[4], [5], [6]]. This drug delivery mechanism achieved PTX levels in the tumor bed up to 2000-fold that of systemic intraperitoneal administration equivalent (29,100 ng/g vs 14 ng/g) and additionally achieved these high doses for an extended duration (up to 30 days vs 1 day) [7]. The chemotherapeutic efficacy of local, supratherapeutic PTX delivery was agnostic to the canonical mechanism of action of microtubule stabilization and cell cycle arrest [8]. Prior studies have shown that PTX’s mechanism of action is modulated in a concentration- and time-dependent fashion [[8], [9], [10], [11], [12]].

Therefore, the susceptibility of a tumor to therapy and the ability to overcome resistance depends on the conditions in which the drug is applied. Furthermore, supratherapeutic PTX doses delivered in vitro are lethal and in vivo studies do not allow for facile delivery of these supratherapeutic, prolonged doses. Organotypic culture was employed for delivery of sustained, high dose chemotherapy to model the therapeutic efficacy of sustained, supratherapeutic PTX. We hypothesized that sarcoma tumor slices will exhibit resistance to PTX at systemic equivalent doses but demonstrate sensitivity at supratherapeutic doses, mirroring the in vivo buttress system. Additionally, we aimed to highlight key molecular players for chemosensitivity important in the administration of supratherapeutic PTX. This study serves as a proof of principle for tumor-drug response model development, which may in the future serve as a precision tool for testing existing and novel therapies.

## Materials and methods

### Organotypic culture model setup

Liposarcoma cells (LP6) locally derived from a dedifferentiated liposarcoma resected specimen were cultured in DMEM/F12 media supplemented with 10 % FBS, 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 mg/mL streptomycin (Gibco, Catalog No 11,320,033, ThermoFisher). Cells were cultured at 37 °C and 5 % CO2. This cell line was chosen as liposarcoma encompasses the most common histologic retroperitoneal sarcoma subtype and a well-established two-dimensional monolayer and small animal local recurrence model exist with this cell line. Paclitaxel tumor penetration in various tumor tissues is reported to be up to 100 μm without cancer cell death and 150 μm with cancer cell death (Kyle 2007).

All in vivo work presented in this study was approved by the Massachusetts General Hospital Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. Two million LP6 cells were subcutaneously inoculated in the dorsum of Nu/J mice (Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, ME). Mice were euthanized when tumors reached 1000 mm3. Untreated LP6 tumor slices were cut at 250 µm thickness using a VT1200S vibratome (Leica Biosystems, Germany) with an amplitude of 0.3 mm at a frequency of 0.22 mm/second (Fig. 1A) [13]. Punch biopsies (8 mm or 6 mm) of mounted tumor specimens were performed to allow for homogenous tissue area and volume within and between tumor slices. ### Organotypic culture model validation and tumor slice viability

Model viability at various days of model duration (day 0 to 10) was established with 3-(4,5-Dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-5-(3-carboxymethoxyphenyl)-2-(4-sulfophenyl)-2H-tetra-zolium (MTS) (CellTiter 96® AQueous One, Catalog No G3582, Promega), trypan blue, and amine reactive dye via flow cytometry.

A standard MTS assay was utilized for in vitro tumor slice measurement of cell viability to establish organotypic culture model validity according to the following protocol [14]. Briefly, at the chosen time point, tumor slices were transferred to a 24-well plate with DMEM/F12 media with FBS. After 2-hour incubation, colorimetric reading at 490 nm was performed with Infinite 200pro MPlex plate reader (TECAN, Switzerland). Viability was calculated as a percentage of absorbance for tumor slices from day 0 timepoint.

For both trypan blue and flow cytometry, tumor slice dissociation to achieve a single cell suspension was performed [15]. In brief, the tumor slices were first mechanically, then, enzymatically dissociated with 0.25 % trypsin-EDTA and DNase I (0.2 mg/mL) at 37 °C for approximately 30 min with trituration with a wide-bore pipet tip every 10 min. After quenching 1:1 with DMEM supplemented with 10 % FBS, cells were filtered through a 70 μm filter (Easystrainer, Catalog No 542,170, Grenier). Viability was confirmed with trypan blue staining (Gibco, Catalog No 15,250,061, ThermoFisher) on a TC20 Cell Counter (Bio-Rad). For flow cytometry, the single cell suspension was washed with FACS buffer and sequentially incubated with amine reactive viability dye (LIVE/DEAD™ Fixable Near-IR Dead Cell Stain Kit, Catalog No L34975, 1.25:100 μL, ThermoFisher) then CD44 monoclonal antibody (Hermes-1 Super Bright™ 702, Catalog No 67–0445–82, 1.25:100 μL, eBioscience, ThermoFisher), following the manufacturer’s protocol; then, the samples were fixed in 2 % formaldehyde for 30 min. Compensation was routinely performed in order to account for fluorophore spillover between markers across detectors (UltraComp eBeads Plus Compensation Beads and ArC Amine Reactive Compensation Bead Kit, Catalog No 01–3333–41 & A10628, ThermoFisher). Analysis was performed on Attune CytPix (ThermoFisher) in FACS buffer. At least 20,000 cells per sample per replicate were counted. The following gating strategy was used: first, scatter gating was performed to exclude debris and select the general population of cells, then doublet exclusion gating as well as a second check for singlets was performed in all experiments. Subsequently, depending on the experiment, either live/dead or CD44+ gating was performed. This has been specified in corresponding figure legends.

### Tumor slice microenvironment characterization

Tumor slice microenvironment characterization was performed via staining with CD44, a cell surface adhesion protein overexpressed in sarcoma [16]. Other markers, such as MDM2, which is known to be amplified and overexpressed in liposarcoma, and a murine haplotype of MHC-I to identify murine cells, were tested, but exhibited either non-specific binding or poor receptor affinity in the stroma.

### Drug response

Tumor slice cell viability in response to varying concentrations (0.1 ng/mL to 30,000 ng/mL) and exposure time (day 1 to 5) of PTX was established via MTS and flow cytometry. The above parameters, conditions, and reagents were used. PTX was solubilized in 1:1 Cremophor EL/ethanol (PTX C/E).

### Gene expression array processing and statistical analysis

Differential gene expression was examined using the TaqMan Human Molecular Mechanisms of Cancer gene array (Catalog No 4418,806, ThermoFisher), which includes 92 key genes commonly implicated in oncogenesis. This gene array was chosen to focus on pathways implicated in cancer cell death. After PTX treatment, tumor slices were harvested for RNA extraction. Each treated tumor slice was paired with an untreated control slice to account for transcriptional drift. Additionally, tumor slices were analyzed after day 1 and day 4 of incubation to capture genetic changes that occurred prior to late-stage cell stress, given that viability remains greater than 50 % at day 4 in both untreated and treated tumor slices (Fig. 1, Fig. 3). RNA integrity was analyzed with NanoDrop Spectrophotometer (ThermoFisher) prior to proceeding with the array. Following reverse transcription (High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit, Catalog No 4368,814, ThermoFisher), quantitative PCR was performed on a QuantStudio 3 (Applied Biosystems). Background subtraction and transcript normalization were completed with the robust multi-array average algorithm via the Design and Analysis software (ThermoFisher). Fold change values for genes were calculated as the ratio of the signal values of the PTX treated groups compared with the untreated groups at a given study day. Ratios of ≥2 or ≤2 reflected genes that were considered statistically significantly differentially expressed using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to determine statistical significance. Multiple paired t-tests were performed on the average delta cycle time for each condition (day 1 and day 4) with comparison of drug-treated vs. control. Individual variance was assumed for each group and a normal Gaussian distribution was assumed. Multiple comparisons were controlled with false discovery rate (FDR) via two-stage step-up (Benjamini, Krieger, and Yekutieli) with desired FDR of 5 %. Pathway gene set enrichment analysis of a ranked gene list was implemented using WEB-based Gene SeT AnaLysis Toolkit (WebGestalt, 2024) utilizing the WikiPathways cancer and Reactome functional database with a p-value cutoff of 0.05.

Technical validation was performed in this study by performing 5 biological replicates and 2 technical replicates. Normalization was performed with GAPDH as the housekeeping gene, a validated housekeeping gene. Stable expression of GAPDH was seen across replicates and conditions.

### Caspase functional assay

After treatment, organotypic slices were dissociated according to above protocol and stained with Vybrant fluorescence inhibitor of caspase (FLICA) reagent (Catalog No V35119, ThermoFisher) according to manufacturer specifications along with CD44 and amine reactive viability dye as mentioned above. Caspase 8 activity was quantified under various treatment conditions using the Attune CytPix flow cytometer (ThermoFisher).

### Specimen repository

Liposarcoma organotypic tumor slices of 8 mm harvested per above protocol and treated with 0 to 30,000 ng/mL PTX between 1 and 4 days were snap frozen in OCT compound with isopentane and liquid nitrogen to create a repository of samples for future experimentation.

### Statistical analysis

Continuous variables were analyzed using two-tailed Welch’s t-test or one-way ANOVA, where appropriate and normality assumptions were met. In the case of lognormal or other distribution, lognormal Welch’s t-test, non-parametric Mann-Whitney test, or Kruskal-Wallis test was used. Bonferroni post-hoc analysis was used for ANOVA testing. Simple linear regression was performed via least squares goodness of fit. Categorical variables were analyzed using Chi-square test. GraphPad Prism 10.0 was used for the analysis. A two-sided p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

### Data availability

Raw and derived data supporting the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon request.

## Results

### Parameters for organotypic culture slices

Given the adipose rich composition of the tumor, slice integrity was best maintained at 250 μm slice thickness with 0.22 mm/s cutting speed. Thinner slices or faster cutting led to tissue disintegration and uneven slices. Additionally, the entire tumor specimen was loaded onto the platform, and punch biopsies were performed to ensure a relatively homogenous tissue slice area (Fig. 1A). 8 mm diameter tumor slices were the largest that could be cultured. Supplemental Figure 1 demonstrates slice to slice variability for viability at day 0.

### Cellular viability

Tumor slice viability was maintained from day of harvest (day 0) to day 10 (around 40 %) as measured daily by several assays (Fig. 1F-H). Viability remained greater than 60 % up to day 5 in both 8 mm and 6 mm diameter slices both via colorimetric and flow cytometric measurements. There was no statistically significant difference in viability between tumor slice sizes (p-value = 0.8598, mixed-effects model with stacked matching). Viability decreased with time by 5.6 % per day via MTS (p-value < 0.0001, simple linear regression) and 11.3 % per day via flow cytometry (p-value = 0.0004, simple linear regression). Lower viability was observed via flow cytometry as compared to MTS (49 % vs 62 % at 4 days), although not statistically significant (p-value = 0.5767) likely due to cell death during flow cytometry staining and sample preparation (Fig. 1I-K). Viability was consistent between MTS and trypan blue measurement (63 % vs 66 % at 4 days; p-value = 0.0725 for comparison between slopes), which occurred immediately after tissue dissociation and demonstrated that significant cell death did not occur due to dissociation. Thereafter, the remainder of assays performed were done on or before day 5 to ensure greater than 60 % of cells were viable at the time of experimentation. 8 mm tumor slice diameter was used for the remainder of experiments given similar viability to 6 mm tumor slice diameter and increased yield of cells per slice with larger slice (optical density: 1.125 vs 0.714 for 8 mm vs 6 mm p-value = 0.002; total cells/slice: 2.06 × 106 vs 9.22 × 105 for 8 mm vs 6 mm p-value = 0.0012; live cells/slice: 1.73 × 106 vs 8.73 × 105 for 8 mm vs 6 mm p-value = 0.001) (Supplemental Figure 1D).

### Xenograft slice composition

Tumor slice composition was examined by flow cytometry. Given human tumor cell line injection into a murine model, a xenograft population was expected. Tumor slices were composed of primarily CD44+ cells (82 % ± 7 %) derived from human LP6 cancer cells. Human cell CD44 staining was confirmed with in vitro LP6 cells (positive control, 97 % ± 0.1 %), while a murine cancer cell line was used as a negative control for CD44 staining (0.2 % ± 7.2 %) (Fig. 2). ### Paclitaxel dose response

Tumor slice viability in response to PTX was compared to 2-dimensional in vitro LP6 monolayer (IC50 8.17 ng/mL at 5 days). The amount of drug delivered was limited by the solubility within the solvent (Cremophor/ethanol) and the cell toxicity (0.1 % to 0.5 % in DMSO). No drug response was seen with MTS even at high concentrations (30,000ng/mL) and prolonged duration (5 days) (viability 117 % ± 10 %). Although there was variability in percent viability with average values ranging between 82 % and 137 % for the entirety of the data set for the MTS assay, the overall trend did not demonstrate the expected sigmoidal distribution of the dose-response curve seen with PTX exposure in monolayer culture. However, a decrease in cell viability was seen with flow cytometry at elevated concentrations (10,000 ng/mL or greater) and prolonged duration (3 days or greater) (Fig. 3A-B) (viability 24 % ± 10 %). ### Differential gene expression and gene set enrichment analysis

Organotypic LP6 tumor slices were exposed to high-dose (10,000ng/mL) PTX for varying durations (1 day and 4 days). Subsequently, expression of key genes known to be involved in cancer pathways was examined. A subset of 17 genes (18S, BAX, BCL2L11, CASP8, CCNE1, ELK1, ERBB2, FZD1, LEF1, MYC, NFKBIA, PIK3R1, PTEN, PTK2B, SHC, SPP1, TCF3, ITGA2B) (Table 1) were significantly differentially expressed as compared to untreated controls after 4 days of treatment; while no genes were differentially expressed after 1 day of treatment (Fig. 4A-C). Gene set enrichment analysis revealed this differentially expressed gene set to be enriched in apoptosis (normalized enrichment score = 1.58, p-value = 0.044), integrin cell surface interaction (normalized enrichment score = 1.72, p-value = 0.022), T cell factor (TCF) dependent signaling in response to Wingless-related integration site (WNT) (normalized enrichment score = 1.65, p-value = 0.029), signal transduction (normalized enrichment score = 1.67, p-value = 0.033), extracellular matrix (ECM) organization (normalized enrichment score = 1.63, p-value = 0.035) pathways. While this differentially expressed gene set was de-enriched in cell motility and invasiveness (normalized enrichment score = −1.79, p-value = 0.02), senescence associated secretory phenotype (normalized enrichment score = −2.32, p-value = 0.0037), non-integrin membrane-ECM interactions (normalized enrichment score = −2.02, p-value = 0.0068), cell cycle regulation via RB1 (normalized enrichment score = −1.62, p-value = 0.028) pathways with both pro- and anti-tumor genes (Web Gestalt, Fig. 4D-E). The apoptosis pathway was further constructed and highlights (in blue) many differentially expressed genes found in this cohort (Fig. 4F). Specifically, NFKBIA, BAX, MYC, CASP8, and PIK3R1 were significantly upregulated. ### Caspase 8 functional assay

Given prior work describing PTX activated caspase activation and our findings of differential upregulation of caspase 8 with high dose and duration PTX treatment, functional validation of caspase 8 was pursued via flow cytometry of enzyme substrate activity. Compared to two-dimensional monolayer control of LP6 cell line, which demonstrated early activation of caspase within a subset cell population at low levels of PTX treatment with 10 ng/mL (65 % vs. 0.1 % of dying or dead cells demonstrated caspase 8 activity for monolayer vs. organotypic, respectively), organotypic liposarcoma tumor slices demonstrated caspase 8 activation only at levels of 10,000 ng/mL of PTX or greater after 4 days of treatment (39 % for 10,000 ng/mL PTX and 75 % for 30,000 ng/mL PTX of dying or dead cells demonstrated caspase 8 activity) (Fig. 5). CD44-positive cells demonstrated a trend towards positive association between increasing PTX concentration and amount of caspase positivity; however, it was not statistically significant (p-value = 0.190 for slope, R2 = 0.91 via simple linear regression) in a descriptive analysis. ## Discussion

In this work, we establish a facile, feasible ex vivo model system to replicate clinical scenarios and test therapies that are challenging to study in vitro or in vivo. An organotypic slice culture derived from a liposarcoma human cell line via murine implantation demonstrates resistance to a chemotherapeutic agent unless treated with high doses, >1000-fold needed for cytotoxicity with a two-dimensional monolayer, and for prolonged duration. This mimics clinical RPS lack of response to PTX with systemic administration. We also demonstrate how to overcome this therapeutic inefficacy as in the investigational in vivo scenario of localized drug delivery depots, by which sensitivity is seen with supratherapeutic doses for extended duration [7]. Thus, this model system serves as a bridging technology to investigate pertinent preclinical and clinical questions in a representative tumor microenvironment that would be otherwise limited by drug toxicity, feasibility, and other constraints inherent to in vitro or in vivo systems. Additionally, organotypic culture given its efficient model establishment as compared to other techniques, such as patient avatar techniques that rely on animal implantation and patient-derived xenografts, may be considered as a platform for testing patient-specific susceptibility to different anti-cancer agents in the future and, therefore, could be promising for the development of precision therapy [[17], [18], [19], [20], [21], [22]].

Several studies report PTX’s differential mechanism of action at concentrations of 100 nM (85 ng/mL) with microtubule dynamic suppression rather than induction as well as increased intracellular drug accumulation [[23], [24], [25]]. At even higher doses between 8000 nM (6831 ng/mL) to 50,000 nM (42,695 ng/mL) further distinctions in mechanism are noticed with microtubule bundling, inhibition of S phase entry, reactive oxygen species generation, and necrosis rather than apoptosis [[26], [27], [28]]. In this study, we find that exposure to high concentrations is necessary, but not sufficient for organotypic slice toxicity as toxicity is time dependent as well. This time dependency may be due to the reliance of PTX’s mechanism of action on microtubule disruption primarily occurring in the M phase of the cell cycle. Inter-assay variability between MTS and amine reactive dye used in flow cytometry likely stems from the mechanism used to detect cell death. MTS relies on reduction of tetrazolium by mitochondrial dehydrogenase in metabolically active cells, while the amine reactive dye used in this flow cytometry is sensitive to early membrane integrity loss. In particular, PTX may not alter metabolic activity especially in early stages as mitochondria may remain active despite apoptosis initiation [[29], [30], [31]]. Additionally, other studies demonstrated that tetrazolium reduction assays, such as MTS, may fail to confirm induction of caspase-mediated cell death [32].

To our knowledge, there are no studies examining differential gene expression with supratherapeutic PTX administration. We investigate a subset of genes, focusing on those commonly implicated in cancer cell death pathways and, that therefore, may play a role in the increased efficacy of sustained, high-dose PTX administration. The identified enriched gene set contains key players in apoptotic, senescent, proliferative, extracellular matrix, cell motility, and cell cycle pathways and represents a heterogenous group of both pro- and anti-tumor genes. Some of these genes have been previously implicated in PTX’s mechanism of action or resistance, while other genes have not been previously described (Table 1). We hypothesize that the upregulation of CCNE1 allows cells to evade PTX-induced mitotic arrest by accelerating G1/S progression, whereas PTX targets G2/M, and, therefore, contributes to resistance [33]. CCNE1 amplification has been associated with poor taxane response and CDK2 inhibitors, such as dinaciclib, have been shown to counteract CCNE1 resistance [[34], [35], [36], [37], [38]]. Caspase 8 plays an important role in PTX-mediated apoptosis [[39], [40], [41]]. Specifically, extrinsic apoptosis triggered via caspase 8 activation occurs only at supratherapeutic concentrations of 10,000 ng/mL PTX with organotypic slice cultures, while present at therapeutic concentrations of 10 ng/mL PTX with traditional monolayer culture. This study identifies potential involved pathways that are both shared and distinct pathways of cell death occurring with supratherapeutic PTX administration as compared to therapeutic doses administered when studying monolayer culture or with systemic administration [[42], [43], [47]]. This differentially expressed gene set was identified after 4 days of treatment with high dose (10,000 ng/mL) PTX in comparison to traditional monolayer studies, which observe genetic changes as early as 16 h and with doses as low as 1 ng/mL [[44], [45], [46]]. Preliminarily, this serves as proof of principle that organotypic culture can serve to efficiently distinguish differential involved mechanistic genetic differences from classical 2-dimensional monolayer as well as evidence that the pharmacodynamics of a chemotherapeutic occur on a different timeframe in classical monolayer and organotypic slices.

Limitations include the finite duration of ex vivo slice cultures that, therefore, cannot replicate in vivo administration periods of 30 days or greater. Organotypic slices have a finite thickness and, therefore, there is a diffusion gradient of nutrients, oxygen, and drug across the tumor slice. We partially mitigated this by complete submersion of slices within the culture media. Additionally, organotypic culture does not capture key in vivo factors such as immune infiltration, vascularization, and extracellular matrix density. Although utilizing gene arrays provides a convenient, targeted method for profiling gene expression across a predefined gene set of interest, the limited gene coverage may result in missing findings regarding relevant genes not included in the array. Additionally, this model is derived from a single cell line and incorporates xenograft stroma. Future studies should include a more comprehensive gene expression analysis, protein and functional validation of the identified differentially expressed genes, specifically caspase 8 with functional perturbation, investigation of resistance mechanisms, and utilization of other cell lines or patient tumors, which although more representative of human biology, is limited by accessibility and reproducibility.

## Conclusion

A reproducible, representative organotypic culture model of liposarcoma exhibited drug resistance at conditions mimicking systemic administration but demonstrated susceptibility at sustained supratherapeutic conditions, such as those achieved by localized drug delivery systems, via modulation of apoptotic pathways. This model serves as a proof of principle both for the efficacy of localized drug delivery, which may be agnostic to a therapy’s canonical mechanism of action as well as potential for personalized tumor-specific therapy testing via organotypic culture model systems.
